newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH MARKET, OFFICIAL RATES DUE TO RISE- C.BANKER.
newsitem.headline: POLISH MARKET, OFFICIAL RATES DUE TO RISE- C.BANKER.

text.p: Poland's central bank will raise market rates further and very likely up nominal rates to counter credit growth and offset effects of extra central bank financing of flood relief, the bank's head said on Thursday.

Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz told Reuters that the central bank, which has long warned it would be tightening monetary policy to contain booming credit, would pursue an even more restrictive policy to offset effects of its financing of the relief effort.
"Even before the flood, actions were needed to limit money supply and the disaster makes such actions even more necessary," the National Bank of Poland (NBP) president said.

"Real interest rates will keep on growing and we should forget for many months about rate cuts and there is a very real possibility of a rise in nominal rates," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said in an interview.
"Credit growth is still high and market rates are so close to the lombard rate that everything indicates that we will have to raise nominal rates," she added.

On Thursday the lower house of parliament authorised the government to borrow an extra 2.5 billion zlotys from the central bank to finance relief operations and remove the damage of 11-day flooding which has claimed 46 lives and inundated 4,500 sq kms.

The government vowed it would not boost this year's planned 2.8 percent deficit but Gronkiewicz-Waltz said extra government financing in the central bank would nevertheless create a monetary impulse which called for more monetary tightening.
"We will be neutralising the impact of the credit with standard instruments such as open market draining operations, interest rates and mandatory reserves," she said.

In order to tighten its grip on money supply, the central bank has kept its official lombard and discount rates, now at 25 percent and 22 percent respectively, unchanged since July last year despite a steady fall in inflation.
Twice this year the NBP has also increased obligatory reserve requirements for banks to contain monetary expansion.

But despite the central bank's efforts, money supply grew 11.3 percent in the first half of the year, faster than planned, with credit expanding by 16.5 percent or 13.39 billion zlotys over the period.
